title: Orbital Knitwear
tagline: Tune a satellite's orbit and knit the planet in wool, one pass at a time, while the flat map lies about the holes.
description: Tune a satellite's height, tilt and orbit shape and watch its ground track knit a wool-textured world map, one ribbon of stitches per pass, in a flat or a polar view. Eight pattern cards set goals such as seeing latitudes the space station never reaches, repeating the same track every 16 days, or keeping one local time of day. Scores count true surface area, so the map's inflated poles cannot flatter you.

sources.title: Sun-Synchronous Orbit | Spacecraft Design Interview | Skill-Lync Resources
International Space Station Frequently Asked Questions - NASA

makingOf: Up to three satellites fly a two-body orbit with the J2 correction: Earth's bulge slowly turns each orbit's plane and perigee. Each pass is painted into a one-degree grid of stitches as wide as the satellite's swath, and scores weigh every stitch by its true area, so polar holes that look huge on a flat map count for little. The model is checked against figures from NASA, ESA and USGS pages and one independent explainer, found through web search and cross-checked between results (the team did not open every page): it gives 97.79 and 98.19 degrees of tilt for a sun-synchronous orbit at 600 and 700 km, and a 233-orbits-in-16-days repeat at about 699.6 km against Landsat's 705 km. It is a toy, not a tracker: tracks drift from real satellites over weeks, coastlines are hand-simplified, pars were found by brute-force search with this model, and the sun moves uniformly along the ecliptic.
